stem: A CI system authenticates tens of thousands of short pipeline jobs per hour. Each job reads a few secrets and finishes in minutes, and nothing needs to renew, revoke or create child tokens. Which token type reduces storage load on Vault the most?

choices.text: Batch tokens, because they are encrypted blobs that need no storage writes when they are created.
Root tokens with a use limit, because root tokens bypass the token store when they are generated.
Service tokens with a short TTL, because Vault removes their storage entries immediately after the last use.
Periodic service tokens, because the fixed period lets Vault skip tracking each token in its token store.

stem: Which statement about batch tokens, compared with service tokens, is accurate?

choices.text: A batch token can create child tokens, which expire together with it.
A batch token can be revoked early by looking up its accessor and revoking that accessor.
A batch token is always issued with a fixed TTL and cannot be renewed to extend it.
A batch token can be created as periodic when the role sets a period value.

stem: An application obtained a token with `vault token create -type=batch -ttl=15m`. After ten minutes it runs `vault token renew` and gets an error. What explains the failure?

choices.text: The application first has to call the renewal endpoint with the accessor, which batch tokens return at creation.
Batch tokens can only be renewed after the first half of the TTL has passed, and ten minutes is too early.
The token must be created with the `-period` flag before Vault will accept renewals for it.
Batch tokens are not renewable, so the application must request a new token before the TTL ends.

stem: A platform team runs Vault with performance replication and wants orphan tokens that clients can use against any performance cluster. Which choice fits, and what is the trade-off?

choices.text: Root tokens, accepting that they need a quorum of unseal key holders for every creation.
Batch orphan tokens, accepting that they cannot be renewed or revoked individually.
Periodic service tokens, accepting that the period must be identical on every cluster.
Service tokens, accepting that they are written to storage on every cluster that serves the client.

stem: A release pipeline creates one token per deployment for a deploy agent. The agent must be able to start a helper process that gets its own sub-token, and an operator wants to revoke the agent's access mid-run if needed. Which token fits?

choices.text: A recovery token, because it is the only type meant for short-lived automation.
A service token, because it can create child tokens and can be revoked before it expires.
A batch token with `-orphan`, because orphan batch tokens can create their own children.
A batch token, because an operator can revoke it on its own with `vault token revoke`.

stem: A new administrator asks what makes a root token different from the other tokens a Vault cluster issues. Which statement about root tokens is accurate?

choices.text: A root token has the `root` policy attached and is the only token that can be set to never expire.
A root token always has a 32 day TTL so that a forgotten one revokes itself.
A root token can be created by any token whose policy grants `create` on `auth/token/create`.
A root token is a batch token with an added `root` policy, so it needs no storage.

stem: Which TWO of the following are documented ways to create a root token? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Enabling the `userpass` auth method and assigning the `root` policy to a user.
Running `vault token create -policy=root` with a token that has the `default` policy.
Running `vault login -method=token` with any token that has `sudo` on `auth/token/create`.
Running `vault operator init`, which prints the initial root token.
Running `vault operator generate-root` with a quorum of unseal key holders.

stem: All operators lost the root token, and the production cluster is healthy and unsealed. Which action produces a new root token without restarting Vault?

choices.text: Run `vault token create -policy=root` using any token that has the `admin` policy attached to it.
Run `vault operator init` again so that Vault prints a brand new initial root token for the team.
Start it with `vault operator generate-root -init`, then have key holders submit shares up to the threshold.
Restart the nodes in dev mode so that Vault creates a fresh root token on every startup.

stem: During `vault operator generate-root`, the team passes `-otp=<value>` when they start the attempt. What is the OTP for?

choices.text: It authenticates each unseal key holder, so only people with that code can submit key shares.
It replaces the unseal key threshold, so a single holder can finish the attempt with the OTP.
The final root token is XORed with it, so you recover the real token with `-decode` and the same OTP.
It sets how many seconds the new root token stays valid before it is revoked automatically.

stem: Which practice best matches HashiCorp's guidance for root tokens in a production cluster?

choices.text: Use a root token only for initial setup or emergencies, then revoke it and generate a new one later if needed.
Give the root token a short TTL and renew it automatically from a scheduled job.
Keep one root token for each administrator so audit logs can tell users apart.
Store the initial root token in a shared secret store so any on-call engineer can use it daily.

stem: An admin finishes initial setup using the root token and wants to remove it. Which command revokes the root token currently set in `VAULT_TOKEN`?

choices.text: `vault token renew -increment=0`
`vault operator generate-root -cancel`
`vault operator seal`
`vault token revoke -self`

stem: An auditor sees that every `vault token create` response includes both a `token` and a `token_accessor` field. What is a token accessor?

choices.text: The policy name that Vault attaches to a token so that it can read its own details.
A reference returned at token creation that allows limited actions on the token without exposing its ID.
A second secret that must be sent together with the token to authenticate on every request.
A hash of the token that Vault stores in the audit log as the secret value of the token.

stem: A scheduler creates a token for each job and stores only the accessor. Which TWO actions can it perform later with just that accessor? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Read secrets on behalf of the job by presenting the accessor as the client token.
Revoke the token when the job completes, using `vault token revoke -accessor <accessor>`.
Add new policies to the existing token by supplying the accessor and a policy name.
Print the original token ID again, using `vault token lookup -accessor <accessor>`.
Look up the token's properties, using `vault token lookup -accessor <accessor>`.

stem: A security team needs to list every active token in a Vault cluster for an audit. Which statement about this is accurate?

choices.text: The only way to list tokens is `auth/token/accessors`, which returns accessors rather than tokens.
`vault list auth/token/tokens` returns the token IDs, so auditors can reuse them to log in to Vault.
Vault cannot list tokens, so auditors must parse the audit log for token IDs.
Tokens can be listed only by the root token; every other token gets an empty list.

stem: A developer reads `token_duration 768h` in the output of `vault token create` and asks what the TTL of a Vault service token actually describes. Which is accurate?

choices.text: The time since the token's last use, after which Vault revokes it as inactive.
The total lifetime from creation that can never be extended, no matter how often it is renewed.
The number of times the token can be used before Vault revokes it automatically.
The period of validity since the token's creation or its last renewal, whichever is more recent.

stem: A service token was created with a 1 hour TTL, and the application renews it every 30 minutes. After several weeks a renewal returns a TTL shorter than requested, and later the token stops working. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The 30 minute interval is shorter than the TTL, so Vault treats it as abusive and stops extending.
The token became an orphan, and orphan tokens cannot be renewed after one day.
The token reached the maximum TTL that applies to it, so renewals can no longer extend it.
Vault revokes any token that is renewed more than 48 times in a row.

stem: A token is created with `vault token create -ttl=1h -explicit-max-ttl=4h`. The application renews it each hour. How long can this token live in total?

choices.text: Thirty-two days, because the system max TTL replaces an explicit max TTL.
Indefinitely, because renewing before expiry resets the explicit max TTL each time.
Four hours, because the explicit max TTL is a hard limit that renewals cannot extend.
One hour, because the explicit max TTL applies only if the token is not renewed.

stem: A long-running service keeps a database connection pool and must not lose its Vault token while it is alive, but the token should expire soon after the service is shut down. Which TWO statements about using a periodic token for this are accurate? (Select TWO)

choices.text: If the service stops renewing, the token expires within the period, and its leases are revoked.
Periodic tokens are batch tokens, so renewals are performed by the service without storage.
A periodic token can be created by any token with `create` on `auth/token/create` and no further privileges.
A periodic token can have no TTL at all because the period is only a hint to clients.
Create it with `vault token create -period=2h`; each successful renewal resets the TTL to two hours.

stem: A client received a `403` with `invalid token` and `permission denied` messages when calling Vault with a token that worked yesterday. The token has a 24 hour TTL and was never renewed. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: The policy attached to the token was deleted, which turns every call into an invalid token response.
Vault was sealed and unsealed overnight, and sealing deletes all service tokens.
The client IP changed, and Vault answers an unknown source address with `invalid token`.
The token passed its TTL, so Vault revoked it and rejects it as invalid.

stem: During a design review the team debates whether to use orphan tokens for long-lived integrations. Which statement about orphan tokens is accurate?

choices.text: An orphan token is a token whose parent has expired, so Vault immediately revokes it.
An orphan token has no parent, so it is the root of its own tree and is not revoked with other tokens.
An orphan token is a root token without an expiration, created once at `vault operator init` time.
An orphan token can only be a batch token, because service tokens always have a parent.

stem: An engineer logged in with `vault login -method=userpass username=alice` and then ran `vault token create -policy=app` from that session. Later Alice's session token is revoked with `vault token revoke -self`. What happens to the `app` token?

choices.text: It keeps working, because tokens created with `-policy` are always orphans.
Vault revokes it too, because it is a child of the revoked session token.
It keeps working, because only the leases of the parent are revoked.
It becomes an orphan with the same TTL, and an operator must revoke it separately.

stem: A team rotates the token of a deployment service every day by revoking the old token. Each time, tokens created earlier by that service for other apps stop working and the apps fail. Which change fixes this without changing what the apps are allowed to do?

choices.text: Change the app tokens to batch tokens, which are unaffected by revoking a parent.
Increase the service token's TTL so that the old token is never revoked.
Attach the `root` policy to the app tokens so that they do not depend on the service.
Have the service create the app tokens as orphans, using a role with `orphan` enabled or `create-orphan`.

stem: A platform engineer is reviewing how tokens end up without a parent in a Vault cluster. Which TWO actions create an orphan token? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Writing to `auth/token/create-orphan` with a token whose policy allows it.
Running `vault token create -use-limit=1` with an ordinary child token.
Running `vault token create -policy=app` with a token that is allowed to create child tokens.
Running `vault token renew` on a child token before its parent expires.
Logging in with an auth method other than `token`, such as `userpass`.

stem: A team wants a token for a scheduler that must have only the `batch-jobs` policy, with no `default` policy. Which command creates it?

choices.text: `vault token create -policy=batch-jobs -type=batch`
`vault token create -policy=batch-jobs -orphan`
`vault token create -policy=batch-jobs -no-default-policy`
`vault token create -policy=batch-jobs -use-limit=0 -renewable`

stem: A deployment script needs a credential that works for exactly one request to Vault, then dies. Which creation option provides that?

choices.text: `-renewable=false`
`-use-limit=1`
`-explicit-max-ttl=1`

stem: A team plans to standardize token creation for CI jobs by defining a token store role named `ci`. Which statement about token store roles is accurate?

choices.text: A role can only be used by a root token, because creating against any role always needs `sudo` on the path.
A role at `auth/token/roles/ci` is used with `vault token create -role=ci` and can override request parameters.
A role replaces the `default` policy and must be written in HCL like a policy.
A role stores a token itself, so every `-role=ci` call returns the same token value.

stem: An operator wants workers to create their own tokens for a monitoring job, and these tokens must be periodic and orphan, but workers must not get `sudo` on `auth/token/create`. Which design fits?

choices.text: A role with `period` and `orphan` set, plus a policy allowing `update` on `auth/token/create/monitor`.
A batch token role, because batch tokens can be periodic and orphan when created from a role.
Give workers a policy with `sudo` on `auth/token/create` so they can pass `-period` and `-orphan` themselves.
A shared root token that workers use to create tokens, revoked at the end of every day.

stem: Running `vault token create -period=1h` as a developer returns `permission denied`, while `vault token create -policy=app` works. What explains it?

choices.text: Periodic tokens can only be created with the `-type=batch` flag.
The `-period` flag requires the developer to supply an explicit max TTL as well.
Developers cannot create periodic tokens because periodic tokens are reserved for the `root` policy only, even with `sudo`.
Setting a period needs `sudo` on the create path (or a root token), which the developer's policy lacks.

stem: An application runs `vault read database/creds/readonly` and gets a username, a password and a long identifier. Which value does the application keep so that it can later renew or revoke these credentials?

choices.text: The `lease_id`, since lease commands identify credentials by it
The token accessor, because it names the credential issued by the read request
The username, because Vault indexes every dynamic credential by the database login name
The mount path `database/`, because one lease covers every credential issued from a mount

stem: A lease ID for AWS credentials looks like `aws/creds/deploy/abcd-1234`. Which statement about the structure of lease IDs is accurate?

choices.text: The prefix is always the mount type, so every lease of one engine type shares an identical ID prefix
The prefix is a random string and the final path segment is the role, so IDs reveal nothing about origin
The prefix of a lease ID is the name of the token that requested the secret, so it changes per client
The prefix of a lease ID is the path the secret was requested from, which makes revocation by prefix possible

stem: Which two kinds of items get a lease from Vault? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Batch type authentication tokens
Policies attached to an auth method role
Service type authentication tokens
Static key/value entries written with `vault kv put`
Dynamic secrets, such as database credentials generated on demand

stem: An engineer lost the lease ID of database credentials issued from `database/creds/readonly` and wants to find it from the CLI. Which approach works?

choices.text: Run `vault read database/creds/readonly` again, which returns the original lease ID unchanged
Run `vault list sys/leases/lookup/database/creds/readonly`, which needs sudo capability on that path
Run `vault token lookup -accessor` on the database user, which returns its lease IDs
Run `vault lease list database/creds/readonly`, which any authenticated token may run

stem: Running `vault lease lookup database/creds/readonly/27e1b9a1` prints `expire_time`, `issue_time`, `renewable` and `ttl`. What does this command do?

choices.text: It reports timing and renewability, changing nothing
It prints the secret's username and password again from the stored lease record
It marks the lease as audited so that later renewals are logged
It extends the lease by its default TTL and prints the new expiration

stem: A script must check how much time is left on a lease through the HTTP API instead of the CLI. Which call matches `vault lease lookup`?

choices.text: `POST /v1/auth/token/lookup` with the `lease_id` in the JSON body
`GET /v1/sys/leases/renew` with the `lease_id` as a query string
`POST /v1/sys/leases/lookup` with the `lease_id` in the JSON body
`DELETE /v1/sys/leases/lookup` with the `lease_id` in the JSON body

stem: A developer reads a secret from a version 1 `kv` mount and the response includes a `lease_duration`, but `vault lease lookup` finds no lease for it. What explains this?

choices.text: The lease was created but lookup works only for leases that were renewed at least once
KV issues no lease; the duration is only a hint of how often to check back
The duration is wrong because KV leases are stored per namespace and not per mount
Lookup finds only leases of tokens, while KV leases are tracked by the audit log

stem: A lease has 10 minutes left and the client runs `vault lease renew -increment=3600 <lease_id>`. What TTL does the client request?

choices.text: Seventy minutes, because the increment is added to the 10 minutes left
One hour counted from the original issue time, so about 50 minutes more are granted
Ten minutes, because renewal is capped at the remaining time on the lease
One hour counted from now, so the lease should end up with about 3600 seconds left

stem: A team asks why every dynamic secret must carry a lease even when the credential is meant to stay valid for a very long time. Which reason does the lease documentation give?

choices.text: A lease lets the consumer cache the credential indefinitely because Vault pushes a notification when it changes
A lease encrypts the credential with the requesting token so that only that token can use it
A lease forces the consumer to check in with Vault routinely, which makes audit logs more valuable and key rolling easier
A lease makes the credential static, so it can be stored in the key/value engine and read without renewal

stem: A service asks `vault lease renew -increment=86400 <lease_id>` and the output shows `lease_duration 1h`. What should the operator conclude?

choices.text: The command failed silently and the old lease continues unchanged
The client token TTL overrides the lease and must be raised first
The renewal doubled the lease because lease durations always grow in whole hour steps
The backend capped the request; the returned duration is the lease

stem: `vault lease lookup` on some credentials shows `renewable false`. The application's lease ends in five minutes. How does the application keep working?

choices.text: Wait for expiry, because Vault renews non-renewable leases once
Read the secret's path again to get a replacement before expiry
Run `vault lease renew -force` to override the renewable flag
Revoke the lease with `-prefix` so a renewable lease replaces it

stem: A script holds the lease ID of AWS credentials and must extend them so that about half an hour remains. Which HTTP request does this?

choices.text: `POST /v1/sys/leases/renew` with `{"lease_id": "...", "increment": 1800}`
`POST /v1/sys/leases/lookup` with `{"lease_id": "...", "increment": 1800}`
`POST /v1/auth/token/renew` with `{"token": "<lease_id>", "increment": 1800}`
`PUT /v1/sys/leases/extend` with `{"lease_id": "...", "ttl": 1800}`

stem: A script has the lease ID of a service token and sends it to `POST /sys/leases/renew`, which is rejected. Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: Tokens are not renewed there; `auth/token/renew` is used instead
Token leases can be renewed there only with a root token
The endpoint is disabled by default until an operator runs `vault lease enable` on the cluster
The endpoint renews only batch tokens, which have a lease

stem: Which two statements about renewing a lease for a database credential are accurate? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Renewing a lease issues a new lease ID so the old one is invalidated
A successful renewal always grants the full increment requested
The requested increment is measured from the time of the request, not from the end of the lease
A lease must be revoked and re-read before it can be renewed
The username and password stay the same; only the validity period changes

stem: A script calls `POST /v1/sys/leases/revoke/aws/creds/deploy/abcd-1234` and also sends the JSON body `{"lease_id": "aws/creds/deploy/efgh-5678"}`. Which lease does Vault revoke?

choices.text: The one in the URL path, because the path parameter takes precedence over the body
Neither, because a request that names the lease twice is rejected as ambiguous
Both leases, because Vault revokes every lease named in the request
The one in the body, because the JSON `lease_id` takes precedence over the path parameter

stem: Which command invalidates one set of database credentials immediately?

choices.text: `vault token revoke database/creds/readonly/27e1b9a1`
`vault lease revoke database/creds/readonly/27e1b9a1`, using the full lease ID
`vault lease revoke database/creds/readonly`, passing only the role path
`vault lease renew -increment=0 database/creds/readonly/27e1b9a1`, asking for no time at all

stem: Intrusion detection suggests an attacker may hold AWS keys generated through the `aws/` mount. What is the fastest way to invalidate all of them?

choices.text: `vault lease revoke aws/`, which treats the path as the lease to revoke
Wait for lease expiry, since expired leases cannot be abused
`vault lease renew -increment=1 aws/`, which shortens every lease under the mount to one second
`vault lease revoke -prefix aws/`, which revokes every lease under that path

stem: A security operator can revoke single leases but gets "permission denied" calling `POST /sys/leases/revoke-prefix/aws`. What is missing from the policy?

choices.text: The `sudo` capability on that endpoint path, since prefix revocation is a privileged operation
The `delete` capability on `sys/leases/revoke-prefix/aws`, as sudo is for root tokens only
The `patch` capability on `sys/leases/revoke`, as prefix calls reuse that path
The `list` capability on `aws/creds/*`, because revocation first has to enumerate keys

stem: A DBA manually dropped a database user that Vault had issued. Now `vault lease revoke` on its lease ID keeps failing because the database reports the user is missing, and the lease remains. Which command removes the lease from Vault?

choices.text: `vault lease renew -increment=1` followed by the full lease ID
`vault lease revoke -sync` followed by the full lease ID
`vault lease revoke -force -prefix` followed by the full lease ID
`vault lease revoke -force` followed by the full lease ID, without `-prefix`

stem: An operator compares `revoke-prefix` with `revoke-force` on `/sys/leases`. What distinguishes the force variant?

choices.text: It revokes leases of a single token only, never of a prefix
It ignores backend errors during revocation, for emergencies where cleanup is failing
It skips the sudo check so non-privileged tokens can use it in outages
It keeps the secrets valid in the backend and deletes the lease record on a schedule

stem: A script calls `POST /sys/leases/revoke-prefix/database/creds` and gets a success response, but a few database users still exist a moment later. Which behavior explains this?

choices.text: Revoke-prefix revokes only the first hundred leases it finds on each call
Vault queues the revocations by default, and `sync=true` makes the call wait for them
Success means only that the prefix exists in Vault
The call revokes leases only once their original TTL has fully run out

stem: A service token used to read many database credentials is revoked. What happens to the leases created with that token?

choices.text: Vault revokes every lease created with that token, removing the users
The leases are re-parented to the root token so that applications keep working
The leases run on until their own TTL ends, since leases are independent of the token
Only the most recent lease is revoked because Vault keeps one active lease per token

stem: A lease is never renewed and its TTL runs out. Which two outcomes apply? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The secret becomes a static value that never expires
The lease moves to the parent token, which gets a fresh TTL
Vault can automatically revoke the lease, for example deleting AWS access keys
Vault extends the lease by the engine default TTL so clients keep working
The consumer can no longer be certain the secret is valid

stem: An operator prefers the web interface to revoke a leaked credential. Where does the documentation place lease revocation in the UI?

choices.text: Under the Policies tab, in each policy's settings
Under the Secrets tab, by deleting the secrets engine's role
Under the Tools tab, using the Wrap tool
Under the Access tab of the Vault UI

stem: Which two actions can revoke the lease of a single dynamic secret? (Select TWO)

choices.text: `vault token renew <lease_id>` from the CLI
`POST /v1/sys/leases/tidy` with the `lease_id` in the body
`POST /v1/sys/leases/revoke` with the `lease_id` in the body
`vault kv delete <lease_id>` from the CLI
`vault lease revoke <lease_id>` from the CLI

stem: After a storage incident, an operator suspects that many lease records no longer have a valid token. Which call revokes leases that lack a valid non-expired token in storage?

choices.text: `GET /v1/sys/leases/count?type=irrevocable`, which revokes the leases it counts
`POST /v1/sys/leases/tidy`, used sparingly since it can cause heavy storage I/O
`POST /v1/sys/leases/renew` on each lease to refresh its token link
`LIST /v1/sys/leases/lookup/` to prune the leases it returns

stem: Operators want to know which mounts produce the most irrevocable leases. Which request reports counts per mount point?

choices.text: `GET /v1/sys/leases/count?type=irrevocable`
`POST /v1/sys/leases/lookup` with an empty body
`LIST /v1/sys/leases/lookup/irrevocable`
`GET /v1/sys/leases/count?type=expired`

stem: A team retires the `database/` mount with `vault secrets disable database/` while applications still hold unexpired credentials from it. What happens to those credentials?

choices.text: Vault refuses to disable the mount until every lease under it has expired
They stay valid until their own TTL ends, because disabling only stops new reads
Only credentials that were never renewed are revoked; renewed ones are kept
Vault revokes every secret the engine created, immediately, and removes the engine's data

stem: A new engineer asks what Vault does when a client presents credentials to an auth method such as userpass or LDAP. Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: The auth method verifies the credentials, then Vault applies its policies to later requests using the original username each time
The auth method verifies the credentials, then Vault issues a token that carries the identity and the policies mapped at login
The auth method verifies the credentials, then Vault returns the secrets the caller is permitted to read in the same response
The auth method stores the credentials in the barrier, then Vault issues a lease that the client must renew to stay logged in

stem: An operator runs vault auth enable -path=corp-ldap ldap. Where is this auth method now reachable, and what does a path-based mount allow?

choices.text: At auth/ldap, since the type fixes the mount path and the flag only sets a label
At corp-ldap, outside the auth/ prefix, because custom paths are mounted like secrets engines
At sys/auth/corp-ldap, and only one mount of a given method type is allowed per cluster
At auth/corp-ldap, and the same method type can be mounted again at another path with its own configuration

stem: A team disables the GitHub auth method that contractors used for a month. What happens to contractors who are still logged in through it?

choices.text: They stay logged in, but their policies are reduced to default because the method no longer supplies mappings
They keep working for 24 hours until Vault refreshes its mount table, then every request is rejected
They are automatically logged out, because disabling an auth method also invalidates the tokens it issued
They stay logged in until their tokens expire, because tokens are independent of the method that issued them

stem: A platform team wants developers to log in to Vault from the CLI and the UI with the accounts they already use in their corporate Active Directory. Which auth method fits best?

choices.text: LDAP, which checks passwords against the existing directory and maps its groups to policies
Userpass, because it can import usernames and passwords from an external directory on a schedule
AppRole, because each developer receives a RoleID and SecretID that match the directory account
TLS certificates, because directory users sign in with a client certificate

stem: A company uses Okta-style single sign-on and wants employees to open the Vault UI and sign in with their browser through the identity provider. Which Vault auth method serves this?

choices.text: JWT/OIDC, with an OIDC role that redirects users to the provider and returns verified claims
GitHub, because its personal access token carries the single sign-on provider session
Userpass, because the UI form posts the provider session cookie
AppRole, because the UI exchanges the browser session for a RoleID

stem: A CI system already receives signed JSON Web Tokens from its own platform, and no browser is available. Which approach lets it log in to Vault without a stored password?

choices.text: The cert auth method, because a JWT is a client certificate in PEM format
A userpass entry whose password is the JWT string, since userpass accepts any signed token value
A JWT-type role on the jwt method, verified with discovery-URL keys or static public keys
An OIDC-type role, because it always opens a local browser callback on port 8250

stem: A service running as a pod in a Kubernetes cluster needs a Vault token without anyone copying a secret into the pod. Which auth method fits?

choices.text: Userpass, with the password injected as an environment variable at deploy time
Kubernetes, which validates the pod's service account token against a bound role
GitHub, with a personal access token of the developer who deployed the pod
LDAP, with the cluster's node name used as the bind username

stem: EC2 instances and Lambda functions must log in to Vault with no operator pre-provisioning credentials to them. Which auth method and type is recommended?

choices.text: aws with the ec2 type only, since it is the recommended type for every compute service
approle with a SecretID baked into the machine image so every instance shares it
cert with the instance's public IP address used as the certificate subject
aws with the iam type, signing an sts:GetCallerIdentity request with credentials the workload already has

stem: Services in a private network already hold X.509 client certificates issued by the company CA. Which Vault configuration lets them authenticate with those certificates?

choices.text: Enable the token auth method and upload the CA certificate to the token store
Enable cert auth, register the trusted CA on a role, and let the listener accept client certificates
Enable the approle auth method and set the certificate fingerprint as the RoleID
Enable userpass and use each certificate's serial number as the account username with a shared password

stem: Which TWO auth methods are designed mainly for automated workloads or machines rather than people? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Userpass
GitHub
Kubernetes
LDAP
AppRole

stem: A deployment pipeline needs to give a new application a way to log in with AppRole while limiting the time and number of times the application's login secret can be used. Which role settings do this?

choices.text: bind_secret_id=false, which makes the SecretID single use automatically
token_policies and token_type, which bound the SecretID's lifetime and the uses it allows
role_id_ttl, which expires the RoleID after the first login
secret_id_ttl and secret_id_num_uses on the role, which cap each SecretID's lifetime and uses

stem: Pods in the namespace demo fail to log in with the Kubernetes method, while the same service account works in namespace default. The role has bound_service_account_namespaces=default. What fixes it?

choices.text: Add demo to the role's bound service account namespaces, or write a role that lists it
Re-enable the auth method with -path=demo so that the namespace becomes its mount
Set disable_local_ca_jwt on every pod so Vault ignores the namespace
Give the pods a RoleID, since namespaces other than default need AppRole

stem: Which statement best describes the difference between how humans and machines should authenticate to Vault?

choices.text: People use directory or provider logins, while machines prove a workload identity such as a role
Humans must call the API directly, while machines must use the UI so that every session is recorded
Machines should use the root token so logins never expire, while humans use short-lived tokens only
Humans and machines should share one userpass account per team to keep the entity count low

stem: An audit review finds that five operators log in with the same userpass account. Which problem does this create, and what is the better design?

choices.text: The shared account's policies are merged with each person's group policies, which grants extra access
Audit entries name one entity for all five, so actions cannot be tied to a person; give each their own login
Vault allows one token per userpass account, so four people are locked out; raise a limit
Userpass tokens cannot be audited, so enable the file audit device with a higher log level

stem: A batch job runs at night, starting new containers each time, and must log in to Vault without an operator present. The orchestrator can deliver a one-time wrapped value to each new container. Which pairing is the best fit?

choices.text: GitHub, with the on-call engineer's personal access token injected into each container at start
Userpass, with a password typed by the engineer when each container starts
LDAP, with a bind password stored in the container image
AppRole, with a short-lived response-wrapped SecretID that the container unwraps at start

stem: Which statement about entities and aliases in Vault identity is accurate?

choices.text: An entity is created only when an operator writes it by hand, and logins without an entity are rejected
An alias belongs to the whole auth method type, so every mount of that type shares one alias
An entity is the consolidated identity of a client, and an alias maps one of its accounts on an auth method mount to it
An alias is the consolidated identity, and an entity is the login name used on one auth method mount

stem: An engineer has accounts at two GitHub auth mounts, auth/github-a and auth/github-b, and one at auth/ldap. Which statement describes what Vault allows?

choices.text: An entity may hold two aliases from the same mount but not from different types
One entity can hold all three aliases, because each lives on a different mount
The three accounts are merged into one entity automatically when the usernames match
One entity holds only one alias per auth type, so the two GitHub aliases need two entities

stem: Which TWO statements about policies attached to an identity entity are accurate? (Select TWO)

choices.text: They add capabilities on top of the policies on the token
They apply only to tokens created through the userpass auth method
They are copied into the token when it is created and never change afterward
They replace the policies that were set on the token at login
They are evaluated at request time, so changing them affects tokens already issued

stem: A group in the identity store is configured as an external group with an alias that maps to the LDAP group sre. What does that provide?

choices.text: All Vault entities become members at once, because an external alias applies to the whole mount
Operators add and remove each member by hand, since external groups never track outside systems at all
LDAP users who belong to sre are added to the Vault group at login and renewal
Membership is refreshed in real time every time the LDAP group changes

stem: An LDAP user is removed from the directory group sre, which maps to an external Vault group granting production access. The user's Vault token has hours left. What does Vault do?

choices.text: The token is revoked at once because group removal revokes every child token
The membership is removed instantly because Vault subscribes to directory change events
The membership stays forever until an operator deletes the alias
Membership is dropped only at the next login or renewal, so the policies can apply until then

stem: Group a has subgroup b, and entity e is a direct member of b only. Which policies does e receive from groups?

choices.text: Only the policies of a, because the parent group overrides its subgroups
Only the policies of b, because policies never flow from a parent group to its subgroup members
The policies of b and of a, since subgroup members are indirect members of the parent
None, because entities obtain group policies only through direct membership in external groups

stem: An operator wants to log in with GitHub using the CLI without putting the token on the command line. Which approach works?

choices.text: Export VAULT_TOKEN with the GitHub token and run vault status
Write the GitHub token to auth/github/config before logging in
Run vault login -method=userpass with the GitHub token as the password
Export VAULT_AUTH_GITHUB_TOKEN and run vault login -method=github

stem: An application authenticates with AppRole through the HTTP API. Where in the response does it find the Vault token to use on later requests, and how does it send it?

choices.text: In lease_id, sent in the Authorization header as Basic
In auth.client_token, sent in the X-Vault-Token header
In data.token, sent as a query string parameter
In auth.accessor, sent in the X-Vault-Token header

stem: An operator has enabled AppRole and now wants an application to be able to log in with the CLI. Which sequence of commands comes next?

choices.text: Write a role under auth/approle/role/, read its role-id and create a secret-id
Enable the token auth method, then attach the AppRole to a token role
Read auth/approle/login to receive a SecretID for the application
Write the application's password to auth/approle/users/ and then log in with vault login

stem: After the AppRole login endpoint is called with a valid role_id but without a secret_id, the request fails. The role was created with default settings. Why?

choices.text: The role has bind_secret_id enabled by default, so a SecretID is also required
The RoleID expires after ten minutes unless it is renewed
The default role type also requires a client certificate in addition to the RoleID
AppRole logins are accepted only from the sys/auth endpoint

stem: Which TWO items must be settled before Vault accepts logins through the OIDC flow from both the CLI and the UI? (Select TWO)

choices.text: An LDAP bind DN and password configured under the jwt mount
A localhost redirect URI such as http://localhost:8250/oidc/callback in allowed_redirect_uris
A static SecretID value that both the CLI and the UI send when they sign in
The root token configured as the OIDC client secret at the provider
A UI redirect URI of the form https://{host:port}/ui/vault/auth/{path}/oidc/callback

stem: Which TWO ways of presenting a Vault token on an HTTP API request are accepted? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The Authorization header with the Basic scheme and the token as the password
A token query string parameter on the URL
A Vault-Session cookie set by the login response
The Authorization header with the Bearer scheme
The X-Vault-Token request header

stem: Which TWO auth methods report the login username as the alias name for the entity Vault creates? (Select TWO)

choices.text: TLS certificates
Kubernetes
Userpass
AppRole
LDAP

stem: A new policy named `empty-reader` is written containing only a comment line and no `path` stanzas, and is attached to a user's token. Which statement about that token is accurate?

choices.text: It can read paths under `secret/` only, because that mount is the default target for policies
It can use any path that no policy explicitly denies, because policies only list the exceptions
It gets no permissions from this policy, because Vault policies are deny by default
It is rejected at login, because Vault refuses to attach a policy that contains no rules

stem: A token carries only a policy containing `path "secret/data/app1/*" { capabilities = ["read"] }`. The holder runs `vault kv get secret/app2/db` against a KV v2 mount at `secret/`. What happens?

choices.text: The request is denied, because no stanza in the token's policies matches the path that is requested
The request is denied, but only after Vault asks the auth method to re-evaluate the token
The request succeeds, because read on one application path implies read on sibling application paths
The request succeeds, but the returned fields are redacted until a second policy approves them

stem: A CI job must read a single database password stored at `secret/data/ci/db` in a KV v2 mount. Which policy follows the principle of least privilege?

choices.text: Read and list on `secret/*` so the job keeps working if the secret moves
Read and sudo on `secret/data/ci/db` so the job is never blocked by protection rules
Read, list and update on `secret/data/ci/*` so the job can also rotate the password
Read on `secret/data/ci/db`, the only path and capability the job needs

stem: Which TWO statements about how Vault policies relate to tokens are accurate? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Vault keeps a copy of the corporate directory so that group membership can be mapped to policies without a lookup
Policies are attached when a token is created, so changing a token's policy set means obtaining a new token
Policies must be written in HCL, and a JSON policy document is rejected when it is uploaded
Logging in a second time invalidates the first token, so a user holds only one valid token at a time
A token refers to its policies by name, so changing a policy's rules affects existing tokens the next time they are used

stem: A policy contains `path "secret/foo" { capabilities = ["read"] }` on a KV v1 mount at `secret/`. Which request does it permit?

choices.text: Reading `secret/foo/bar`, because child paths inherit the capability
Reading `secret/foo`, because the stanza names that exact path
Writing a new value to `secret/foo`, because read implies write on that key
Reading `secret/food`, because the path is matched as a prefix

stem: A policy grants read with `path "secret/bar/*"`. Which of these requests would it still NOT cover?

choices.text: Reading `secret/bar/zip/zap/zong`, because depth is capped at three
Reading `secret/bar/zip/zap`, because the glob stops at one segment
Reading `secret/bar/zip`, because only direct children match
Reading `secret/bars/zip`, because the prefix ends with a slash

stem: A team wants to read the `teamb` secret under any single application folder, as in `path "secret/+/teamb"`. Which request matches this stanza?

choices.text: Reading `secret/alpha/teamb/notes`, because the stanza acts as a prefix
Reading `secret/alpha/beta/teamb`, because `+` spans any number of segments
Reading `secret/alpha/teamb`, because `+` fills exactly one segment
Reading `secret/teamb`, because `+` can stand for an empty segment

stem: A policy author wrote `path "secret/data/*/config"` so that every application can read its own `config` secret, but requests are denied. What is the accurate diagnosis and fix?

choices.text: A glob is supported only as the last character of a path, so `+` should replace the middle `*`
The path needs a second trailing `*` after `config`, which turns the middle one into a wildcard
The policy must be written in JSON because HCL does not allow wildcards in the middle of a path
The `list` capability is missing, and adding it will make the middle `*` expand to each folder

stem: An application uses `vault kv get secret/app/db` on a KV v2 mount named `secret`. Which stanza lets it succeed, and nothing more?

choices.text: `path "secret/app/db" { capabilities = ["read"] }`
`path "secret/metadata/app/db" { capabilities = ["read"] }`
`path "secret/data/app/db" { capabilities = ["list"] }`
`path "secret/data/app/db" { capabilities = ["read"] }`

stem: Operators run `vault kv list secret/apps` on a KV v2 mount named `secret` to enumerate the application keys. Which stanza grants that?

choices.text: `path "secret/list/apps/*" { capabilities = ["list"] }`
`path "secret/metadata/apps/*" { capabilities = ["list"] }`
`path "secret/data/apps/*" { capabilities = ["list"] }`
`path "secret/metadata/apps/*" { capabilities = ["read"] }`

stem: Which TWO statements about KV v2 policy paths are accurate? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Permanently destroying specific versions is authorized with the `delete` capability on `secret/data/`
A stanza on `secret/app/*` protects KV v2 secrets exactly as it would on a KV v1 mount
Reading and writing secret versions are authorized on paths that start with `secret/data/`
Metadata paths can be used only by a token that also holds the `sudo` capability
Listing keys and reading version metadata are authorized on paths that start with `secret/metadata/`

stem: A cleanup role must permanently remove one KV v2 secret, `secret/app/db`, including all versions and its metadata, e.g. with `vault kv metadata delete secret/app/db`. Which stanza grants only that?

choices.text: `path "secret/metadata/app/db" { capabilities = ["delete"] }`
`path "secret/destroy/app/db" { capabilities = ["update"] }`
`path "secret/data/app/db" { capabilities = ["delete"] }`
`path "secret/undelete/app/db" { capabilities = ["update"] }`

stem: An application obtains temporary database credentials with `vault read database/creds/readonly`. Which capability must its policy grant on `database/creds/readonly`?

choices.text: `sudo`, because credential generation is root-protected
`update`, because the database is modified
`create`, because new credentials are being created
`read`, because the HTTP request is a GET

stem: An operator's token has `path "sys/audit/*" { capabilities = ["create", "update"] }`, yet `vault audit enable file file_path=/var/log/vault.log` is denied. What is missing?

choices.text: The `read` capability, because Vault must first read the device list
The `patch` capability, because enabling a device changes the audit configuration
The `sudo` capability, because managing audit devices is a root-protected operation
An exact path `sys/audit/file`, because globs are not accepted under `sys/`

stem: An integration partially updates one field of an existing KV v2 secret with an HTTP PATCH to `secret/data/app/db`, and must not be able to replace the whole secret. Which capability on that path fits?

choices.text: `create`, because it permits writing new keys into the secret
`patch`, because it allows partial updates only
`sudo`, because partial writes bypass normal protection
`update`, because it permits changes to the data at the path

stem: Which TWO statements about policy capabilities are accurate? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The `deny` capability takes precedence over every other capability, including `sudo`
A token that holds `sudo` on a path can perform any operation there without other capabilities
The `list` capability must be granted on the exact key name, not on a prefix
Capabilities are named after the internal action that the backend performs, not after the HTTP verb
The keys returned by a list operation are not filtered by policy, so key names should not contain sensitive information

stem: A token holds two policies. The first has `path "secret/data/app/*" { capabilities = ["read"] }` and the second has the identical path with `capabilities = ["create", "update"]`. What can the token do on `secret/data/app/x`?

choices.text: Read, create and update, because the same pattern in several policies is combined as a union
Only read, because the first policy attached to the token is the one that wins
Nothing at all, because two policies that disagree on a path cancel each other out
Only create and update, because the most recently written policy replaces the earlier one

stem: A token holds one policy granting read and update on `secret/data/*` and another granting only read on the more specific `secret/data/app/*`. Which statement about an update to `secret/data/app/x` is accurate?

choices.text: It is denied, because a token cannot hold two policies that both match one request path
It is allowed, because the broader policy grants update and Vault merges capabilities from all matches
It is denied, because only the highest-priority matching pattern applies and it grants no update
It is allowed, because update is granted by at least one attached policy and read does not forbid it

stem: Policy `dev` grants read and list on `secret/data/hr/*` and policy `hr-block` is attached to the same token with `path "secret/data/hr/*" { capabilities = ["deny"] }`. What is the effect on reading `secret/data/hr/salaries`?

choices.text: Reading is allowed, because the first policy grants read and Vault evaluates grants before denials
Reading is denied, because deny takes precedence over any other capability
Reading is allowed only if the token also holds the sudo capability on the same path
Reading is allowed, because deny applies only to policies attached by group membership

stem: Auditors must read every secret under `secret/data/payroll/` and list its key names on a KV v2 mount, but must not write. Which TWO stanzas, used together, meet that? (Select TWO)

choices.text: `path "secret/payroll/*" { capabilities = ["read", "list"] }`
`path "secret/metadata/payroll/*" { capabilities = ["delete"] }`
`path "secret/data/payroll/*" { capabilities = ["create", "update"] }`
`path "secret/metadata/payroll/*" { capabilities = ["list"] }`
`path "secret/data/payroll/*" { capabilities = ["read"] }`

stem: One policy grants read on `secret/data/*`, and another denies `secret/data/+/prod`. A token holding both reads `secret/data/billing/prod`. What happens?

choices.text: It is denied, because `+` always outranks `*` regardless of where either appears
It is denied, because the pattern ending in `*` has lower priority than the one ending exactly
It is allowed, because `*` covers more paths and the broader grant wins
It is allowed, because a grant and a deny on different patterns are merged by union

stem: A token whose policies are `default` and `dev-reader` runs `vault token create -policy=admin`. The `admin` policy exists. What is the result?

choices.text: It succeeds and the child gets admin, since policy names are only checked when a request is made
It succeeds, but admin is silently dropped and the child gets just the default policy
It fails, because a non-root token can assign only policies that it holds itself
It fails, because only a token that holds the sudo capability on `sys/policy/admin` may reference that policy

stem: Each user must have a private KV v2 folder that follows the user even if the user's display name changes. Which stanza gives each user full access to only their own folder?

choices.text: `path "secret/data/{{identity.entity.name}}/*" { capabilities = ["create", "update", "read", "delete"] }`
`path "secret/data/*" { capabilities = ["create", "update", "read", "delete"] }`
`path "secret/data/+/*" { capabilities = ["create", "update", "read", "delete"] }`
`path "secret/data/{{identity.entity.id}}/*" { capabilities = ["create", "update", "read", "delete"] }`

stem: A policy uses `path "secret/data/{{identity.entity.metadata.team}}/app"` and a user's entity metadata has `team` set to `*`. What happens when the user requests `secret/data/anything/app`?

choices.text: Access is denied, because wildcards in the rendered output of a template produce permission denied
Access is granted only for list, because wildcards expand during listing operations
Access is granted, because the rendered `*` matches any team folder
Vault logs a warning and falls back to the policy without the template

stem: A policy file is produced by a pipeline and reaches the administrator on standard input. Which command uploads it as the policy `app-reader`?

choices.text: `vault policy upload app-reader < app-reader.hcl`
`cat app-reader.hcl | vault policy write app-reader -`
`cat app-reader.hcl | vault policy create app-reader`
`vault write sys/policy/app-reader file=app-reader.hcl`

stem: Which TWO commands show the names of all installed policies and print the rules of the policy `dev-readonly`? (Select TWO)

choices.text: `vault policy show dev-readonly`
`vault policy fmt dev-readonly`
`vault policy delete dev-readonly`
`vault policy read dev-readonly`
`vault policy list`

stem: An engineer must write a policy for `vault kv get -mount=secret app/db` on a KV v2 mount and does not know which paths and capabilities it uses. Which approach uses a documented Vault feature?

choices.text: Run `vault policy fmt` on a policy file, which fills in the missing paths for a command
Copy the `default` policy from `vault policy read default` and add `read` on `secret/*`
Add the `-output-policy` flag to the command, which prints the policy the command requires
Run `vault token capabilities` with the root token against the path, and copy its output

stem: Which statement about the built-in `default` and `root` policies is accurate?

choices.text: The `default` policy is attached by default but can be left off with `vault token create -no-default-policy`
The `root` policy can be trimmed to a narrower set of permissions by an administrator editing it
The `default` policy can be deleted by a root token once the team decides that it is no longer needed
The `default` policy is read-only, and Vault overwrites any local edits when the server is upgraded
